fact_claims.verbatim: 8.6 company-wide thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year
6.2% flagship failure rate in the 55°C sustained-heat test
remote shut-off support on 38% of installed units
approximately $42 per unit to add built-in suppression
Northwind had 3 thermal incidents last year that were not reported to a regulator.

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a full incident report within 10 business days. A manufacturer must notify affected customers within 48 hours when the incident indicates a credible safety risk requiring customer action; otherwise, it must include the incident and any resulting safety guidance in its next scheduled customer safety notice.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: A failure rate above 5% is a regulator-notification and corrective-action trigger, not an automatic market ban. Model-specific results must be provided to customers purchasing that model, but individual-company, per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New models introduced 24 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer notification when it is used. For units already installed on the adoption date, manufacturers must provide a plan within 12 months to enable shut-off where technically feasible and complete upgrades or offer an equivalent risk-reduction measure within 6 years.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression appropriate to the battery chemistry and installation environment, unless the regulator approves an equally effective alternative safety measure.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: If a model’s verified thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and submit incident data and a corrective-action plan. The regulator must assess the risk and may require a recall or other proportionate protective action; a recall is mandatory when the regulator determines that continued use presents an unacceptable safety risk that cannot be adequately addressed by less restrictive measures.

document.section_notes: S1 requires reporting of all thermal incidents within 24 hours, with serious-incident customer notice within 48 hours, which is the strongest section. S2 and S5 lack a sales stop and a mandatory numeric recall trigger, since the 5% and 8-per-100k thresholds trigger only review and corrective action. S3 sets a 24-month deadline for new units and a 6-year retrofit window, which favours Northwind's low shut-off coverage.
